_README: Battery tester troubleshooting — Instrumentation spec §11. EVERY entry must offer MULTIPLE possible causes: the health check rejects a single-cause entry, because one symptom must never be presented as proving one cause. Diagnostics are ordered cheapest-and-most-likely first. DRAFT — review before treating as teaching material.

items.symptom: Large IR drop at the start of discharge
items.summary: The voltage steps down sharply the instant the current reverses, and the step is bigger than expected.
causes: Two-wire sensing, so lead and contact resistance are included in the measured voltage
Poor or uneven contact pressure between the electrode and current collector
High electrolyte resistance — low conductivity, insufficient volume, or incomplete wetting
Current collector corrosion or a poor weld/tab connection
Test current higher than the cell can sustain without large ohmic loss
Genuinely high internal resistance of the electrode itself
diagnostics: Check first whether the channel is using two-wire or four-wire sensing, and where the sense leads actually attach. This is the cheapest check and a very common cause.
Repeat at a lower current: a purely ohmic drop scales linearly with current, so plot ΔV against I and look for a straight line through the origin.
Measure the high-frequency intercept of an impedance spectrum and compare with ΔV/I from the step — if they agree, the resistance is real and ohmic.
Re-assemble the cell with fresh contact and repeat. A large change points to assembly rather than material.
Compare against another cell on a different channel to rule out a channel fault.
fixes: Switch to four-wire sensing and attach the sense leads at the cell terminals
Improve contact pressure and clean the contact surfaces
Allow longer wetting before starting the test
Reduce the test current if the ohmic loss is dominating the measurement
If the resistance is genuine, report it — a high internal resistance is a result, not necessarily a fault
safetyNotes: A rising IR drop combined with heating can indicate a developing internal fault. Stop the test and let the cell cool before handling it.

materialNotes.material.na_metal: This record notes sodium counter electrodes degrade over a long half-cell experiment, so a rising overpotential can be the COUNTER electrode failing rather than the material under test.

items.summary: The measured capacity is well below what the material should deliver.
causes: Active material mass entered incorrectly on the instrument — the most common cause and the hardest to spot, because it scales everything consistently
C-rate defined against a nominal capacity that does not apply to this material, so the actual current is far higher than intended
Voltage window too narrow, cutting the measurement short before the material is fully used
Incomplete electrolyte wetting, so much of the electrode is not electrochemically accessible
Poor electrode fabrication — inadequate binder, poor adhesion, or excessive thickness
Poor active-material utilisation at the current used: rate limitation rather than low capacity
Cell assembly problem such as misalignment or insufficient electrolyte
diagnostics: Re-check the mass entered on the instrument against your own independent record. Do this before anything else — it costs nothing and is the most likely culprit.
Confirm the recorded current matches the intended current density given that mass.
Repeat at a much lower rate. If the capacity recovers, the problem is rate limitation, not capacity.
Check the voltage window against the chemistry and confirm the step ended on the voltage limit rather than a time limit.
Rest the cell longer before cycling and repeat, to rule out incomplete wetting.
Build and test a second cell — a fabrication or assembly problem usually will not reproduce identically.
fixes: Correct the mass and recalculate; never re-enter a mass without recording it independently as well
Define the C-rate against a capacity appropriate to this material
Widen the window only if the chemistry and electrolyte genuinely support it
Allow a longer wetting period before the first cycle
Review the electrode formulation and coating if the problem persists across cells
safetyNotes: Do not widen the voltage window beyond the electrolyte's stability range to chase capacity. Decomposition recorded as capacity is both a wrong result and a safety hazard.

materialNotes.material.hard_carbon: This record names a large first-cycle irreversible capacity that varies with precursor and pyrolysis temperature — a capacity below expectation may be the material as made, not the cell as built.
materialNotes.material.v2o5: This record states the accessible capacity depends on where the voltage window is cut and on how many electrons are actually reached. Check the window before suspecting the cell.
materialNotes.material.pba_nafe: This record states real frameworks carry vacancies and coordinated water, so the theoretical denominator is usually wrong — a low capacity here can be a composition difference rather than a performance one.
materialNotes.material.zn_metal: This record makes zinc UTILISATION the number that matters. A capacity computed per gram of a thick foil will always look poor.
materialNotes.material.graphite: This record states LiC₆ is the fully lithiated LIMIT, and whether the last staging step happens at all depends on the potential window, the rate and the electrolyte. A capacity short of 372 may be the window, not the electrode.
materialNotes.material.lco: This record calls roughly half the theoretical capacity accessible in practice, and says the gap is structural stability rather than kinetics — so a number near half of theory is the expected result, not a fault.
materialNotes.material.lto: This record says the low capacity is by construction, not a defect. Before investigating, check the figure is not simply LTO behaving as LTO.
materialNotes.material.nvp: This record notes the same material is quoted at two different theoretical capacities depending on which vanadium couple is counted. A "low" capacity may be a comparison against the three-electron number, which is practically unreachable in a standard electrolyte.

items.summary: Capacity falls faster than expected over cycling, or the cell fails early.
causes: Structural degradation of the active material over repeated cycling
Unstable interfacial layer that re-forms each cycle, consuming charge continuously
Electrolyte decomposition, often because the voltage window is too wide
Dissolution of active material into the electrolyte
Loss of electrical contact as the electrode expands and contracts — binder failure or particle detachment
Current too high for the material, driving mechanical or structural damage
Temperature excursions during the test
diagnostics: Look at coulombic efficiency first. A persistent shortfall points to a continuously consuming process such as electrolyte decomposition or an unstable interface; a sudden drop points to mechanical failure or a short.
Examine the SHAPE of the fade — linear, square-root-like, or a sudden cliff each suggest different dominant mechanisms.
Narrow the voltage window and repeat. If retention improves markedly, the original window was likely outside the stable range.
Reduce the rate and repeat, to test whether the damage is rate-induced.
Compare the CC and CV capacity fractions over cycle life — a growing CV fraction indicates rising impedance.
Post-mortem examination of the cycled electrode if the cause still is not clear.
fixes: Narrow the voltage window to within the electrolyte's stable range
Reduce the cycling rate if degradation is rate-induced
Review binder content and electrode adhesion
Consider electrolyte additives or a different formulation
Control and record the test temperature
safetyNotes: Rapid capacity loss accompanied by swelling, heating or gas evolution means the cell should be taken off test immediately and isolated. Do not continue cycling to 'see what happens'.

materialNotes.material.silicon: This record puts a threefold volume change, particle fracture and an interphase that re-forms every cycle at the centre of the failure mode.
materialNotes.material.lmo: This record names manganese dissolution, accelerating with temperature and with acidic electrolyte decomposition products.
materialNotes.material.nmc111: This record names transition metals dissolving from the cathode and poisoning the anode interphase — so a cathode fault appears as anode degradation.
materialNotes.material.li_metal: This record notes every plating and stripping cycle breaks and re-forms part of the interphase.
materialNotes.material.pb: This record names sulfation — coarse lead sulfate that will not reduce — as the dominant real-world failure.
materialNotes.material.graphite_k: This record warns the electrode may not survive the lattice expansion the larger ion causes, and that potassium metal counter electrodes degrade in ways attributed to the working electrode more often than they should be.

items.summary: The charge or discharge curve does not look like it should — unexpected steps, noise, plateaus in the wrong place, or no plateau at all.
causes: Contact resistance varying during the test, producing steps or noise
Reversed cell polarity
Voltage limits set for a different chemistry
Current setting far from what was intended
Temperature drifting during the measurement
Cell assembly problem — misalignment, separator issue, or insufficient electrolyte
Data acquisition artefacts: current-range switching, or logging too coarse to represent the real shape
Instrument compliance reached, so the requested condition was never achieved
diagnostics: Check the recorded current column against the setpoint. If they differ, the instrument was not doing what you asked, and the curve shape follows from that.
Check the step end-reason for every step — a step that ended on its time limit did not run the experiment you designed.
Confirm polarity and the voltage limits against the chemistry.
Re-plot with a finer logging interval on a fresh run: apparent steps are often an artefact of coarse sampling.
Repeat on a different channel to separate an instrument fault from a cell fault.
Re-assemble a fresh cell and compare.
fixes: Correct polarity, limits or current settings and repeat
Increase the logging density before concluding anything about curve shape
Improve contact and re-assemble
Control the test temperature
safetyNotes: Reversed polarity can damage a cell and in some chemistries is hazardous. Verify connections before starting rather than diagnosing afterwards.

materialNotes.material.nafepo4: This record notes two polymorphs with the same formula and completely different behaviour — an unexpected curve shape may mean maricite rather than olivine.
materialNotes.material.nnfm: This record notes several phase transitions across the sodium range, and that these materials hydrate on air exposure before the experiment starts.
materialNotes.material.lifepo4: This record notes the plateau is so flat that state of charge is nearly unreadable from voltage — a real operational problem, not a fault to chase.
materialNotes.material.mno2: This record states the polymorphs — α, β, γ, δ, λ — share a formula and behave differently, and that the storage mechanism itself is disputed and electrolyte-dependent. An unexpected curve shape may be a different polymorph or a different mechanism, not a fault.
materialNotes.material.graphite_k: This record notes the larger potassium ion expands the lattice far more than lithium does. Staging features that do not match a lithium graphite curve are expected here.

items.summary: More charge comes out than went in — not physically meaningful for an ideal cell, and always worth investigating.
causes: Soft internal short, allowing charge to leak during the charge step so the measured charge capacity is understated
A redox shuttle in the electrolyte carrying charge without storing it
Charge carried over from a previous incomplete cycle
Current or mass entry error affecting the two steps differently
Measurement resolution at the limit, so the difference is within instrument uncertainty
Steps that used different voltage windows or protocols, making the ratio meaningless
diagnostics: Confirm the charge and discharge capacities come from the SAME cycle and the same window.
Check the magnitude — a value at 100.05% may simply be instrument resolution, whereas 110% is a fault.
Look at the open-circuit voltage after a rest: a cell that drifts downwards persistently is self-discharging.
Check whether the effect grows over cycling, which points to a developing short.
Compare against a second cell to rule out a channel or setup problem.
fixes: Investigate and, if confirmed, retire a cell with a soft short — do not continue cycling it
Review electrolyte formulation if a shuttle is suspected
Ensure protocols are identical across compared cycles
Recheck current and mass entries
safetyNotes: A developing internal short can escalate. A cell showing persistent efficiency above 100% together with heating should be taken off test and isolated.

materialNotes.material.sulfur: This record describes the polysulfide shuttle: charge passes without being stored, which is exactly the mechanism that puts an efficiency above 100% on the wrong side of a cycle.

_materialNotes: Why this symptom is worth checking against THAT material — linked only where the material's own record names the cause. These are candidate causes to rule in or out, never a diagnosis: one symptom never proves one cause.
